verdicts.note: Core facts hold against Google pages updated 2026-10-01: default 10,000 requests a day per Cloud project (standard token preparations count too), quota increase only if the app is available on Google Play and the Cloud project is linked in Play Console, PLAY_RECOGNIZED only for Play-distributed copies, closed-test lists of up to 200 x 2,000 users with per-tester opt-in. The recommendation (Play production as the main Android path, GitHub APK for phones without Google services, no student tester lists) passes the lenses. One inference is wrong and the quota argument is overstated, see correction.
verdicts.correction: 'Off-Play copies cannot get PLAY_RECOGNIZED, so the app-not-modified check in line 78 needs Play' is wrong. Android key attestation, already in the plan (lines 589, 683), carries the package name and the SHA-256 digests of the app's signing certificates (attestation version 2 and up, Android 8+), with no daily quota. So the 10,000 cap only binds if Play Integrity stays the gate for GitHub installs, and past the cap the plan's existing path for unverifiable devices (lines 78, 214) applies instead of a hard stop. The quota part is medium, not high. Play-first still stands, on stronger grounds than the quota: no unknown-sources step, no Play Protect prompt, automatic updates, the 2027 verification rollout, and Samsung Auto Blocker (default on for Galaxy phones that shipped with One UI 6.1.1 or later), which only lets Play or Galaxy Store installs through.

verdicts.correction: (1) 'To use one key across stores you must give your own key' is incomplete. The Play help page lists a second documented way: keep Google's key and publish the signed universal APK from Play Console on other channels. Missing the window therefore does not split Play and GitHub for good, so the severity is medium, not high. (2) The 'consider' wording about a separate upload key is in neither source. Reusing the app signing key as upload key is allowed, but Google states the keys 'should be different'. The finding's reasoning (the signing key already sits in EAS for GitHub builds, so a second key protects little) is sound, but the plan must say it chose against Google's advice. recommendation_issues.problem: The recommendation holds, but the reason it gives ('Play Integrity günde 10.000 istekle sınırlı ve bu sınır artırılamıyor, dönem başı kaydına yetmez') is its weakest argument. Key attestation, already in the plan, identifies the app with no quota, and the plan already flags devices it cannot verify. Rest the change on install friction and updates (no unknown-sources step, Samsung Auto Blocker on by default, no Play Protect prompt, automatic updates, 2027 verification). Also note, as a cross-slice item for line 78, that GitHub installs are checked by key attestation and Play Integrity serves Play installs.

Picks the heavier of Play's two documented ways to keep one signature, does not mention the other, and reuses the app signing key as upload key against Google's 'should be different' advice without saying so. With Play as the main path, keeping Google's key and putting Play's signed universal APK on GitHub removes the key that cannot be recovered from our side, removes the PEPK export step, and saves one Android build per release. Its cost is that GitHub depends on the Play account. If the own-key route is kept anyway, the plan needs the guardrail 'Play'in anahtar yükseltme önerisi kabul edilmez', because on Android 17+ a hybrid upgrade changes the app's signing identity.

The branch condition 'Google servisi olmayan telefonda' should be the install source: if Play Store installed the copy, open the Play page, otherwise open the GitHub link. A GitHub copy on a phone that has Google services, sent to the Play page, can only update there if the signatures match (S11-F2).

misses.finding: Samsung's Auto Blocker is on by default on every Galaxy phone that shipped with One UI 6.1.1 or later. While it is on, only Galaxy Store and Play Store installs go through. A browser-downloaded APK is blocked even after the 'install unknown apps' permission is granted. The install steps for the GitHub APK, which line 36 makes the only Android path, never mention this, so students with newer Samsung phones get stuck at install. Under S11-F1 (Play as the main path) these phones install from Play and the problem goes away; it remains only for the GitHub instructions.

misses.finding: Play documents two ways to keep one signature on Play and outside it: give Play your own key, or keep Google's key and distribute the signed universal APK that Play Console produces. The plan and S11-F2 name only the first. With Play as the main path, the second is lighter. The app signing key, which cannot be recovered if lost, never sits with us; a lost upload key can be reset. There is no PEPK export step. The GitHub file is the binary Play signs, so each release needs one Android build instead of an AAB plus an APK. Play's default quantum-ready signing is kept. Its cost: the GitHub APK can only come out of Play Console, so losing the Play account also stops GitHub updates. If the own-key route is kept, the plan needs a guardrail. Google said in March 2026 it will prompt developers to upgrade signing keys at least every two years. On Android 17+, a hybrid upgrade works as a key rotation that makes the new post-quantum key the app's identity, and a GitHub APK signed only with the old key can then no longer update a Play install on those phones.

evidence.quote: If you lose your upload key or suspect that it was compromised, you are not locked out of your app.
You can distribute this APK on other app stores and distribution channels such as websites so that wherever you distribute your app, it's signed with the same key.
Google Play will also start prompting developers to upgrade their signing keys at least every two years.

The platform treats the hybrid block as an implicit key rotation. The platform appends the new classical key to the app's existing signing lineage as the next-to-last key, and treats the new PQC key as the app's current signing identity.
If a developer attempts to update a hybrid-signed app using only one of the hybrid keys as a single signer without a proper rotation, the update fails.

misses.recommendation_tr: İmza yolunu bilerek seçip plana yazarım. Önerim: Play'in ürettiği anahtarı kabul ederim; GitHub'a Play Console'dan indirilen imzalı evrensel APK'yı koyarım. Böylece kaybolunca geri gelmeyen anahtar bende durmaz (yükleme anahtarı kaybolursa sıfırlanır) ve her sürümde tek Android derlemesi yeter. Bedeli: Play hesabı kapanırsa GitHub sürümü de güncellenemez. Kendi anahtarımı Play'e yüklemeyi seçersem, GitHub yolu sürdükçe Play'in anahtar yükseltme önerisini kabul etmem.

misses.finding: The plan prepares a reviewer demo account only for Apple (line 493). Play review, which also covers closed-test releases, needs one too, and its rules are specific: the sign-in must be reusable, valid from any location, and must bypass one-time codes. The plan's teacher login is email-code only (line 69), release builds have no 'show code' setting (line 87), and a student account binds to one phone (line 84). A demo account that follows those rules cannot be reused across reviewers' devices, which is a common rejection cause.

if your app typically requires a 2-Step verification code or One-time password, make sure to provide reusable login credentials that can bypass these requirements.

verdict_reason: No high-severity finding is refuted or unverifiable. The two high findings (F1, F2) are CORRECTED: their core facts hold against Google pages updated 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-01, and both are downgraded to medium. F1's claim that the app check needs Play is wrong because key attestation carries the signing-certificate digests. F2 misses Play's documented universal-APK option. Tally: 5 CONFIRMED (F3, F4, F5, F6, F8), 4 CORRECTED (F1, F2, F7, F9), 0 REFUTED, 0 UNVERIFIABLE. All 24 checked_ok items were re-checked, including every version, date, limit and price: StatCounter CSV for Sept 2026 gives Android below 7 = 1.82% and iOS below 16.4 about 2.3% plus 0.08% other; Expo SDK 57 table; EAS pricing; developer-verification FAQ (2026-09-30); Obtainium API; GitHub limits; Apple fee. No disputes. Expo SDK 58 (npm 'next' 58.0.3, 2026-10-03, stable expected in October) keeps Android 7+ and iOS 16.4+, so line 516 survives the upgrade. Four misses, none high: Samsung Auto Blocker on by default blocks GitHub APK installs (medium, closed by F1's Play-first path); the lighter Play-signed universal APK option and the key-upgrade guardrail (medium); Play reviewer sign-in rules (low); the name and logo rule for Play (low). Accepted recommendations reduce moving parts overall.
